# Diving bell and underwater work (`diving_bell`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by atmospheric_pressure, gas_laws, buoyancy_hydrostatics
- Core idea: Lower a heavy, open-bottomed bell evenly into the water: the trapped air lets people breathe and work on the bottom, but the water compresses it (to half its volume at 10 m, a third at 20 m), so fresh air must be sent down (Halley used weighted barrels; later a pump) and stale air vented. Long exposure to pressure can require staged decompression.
- Pitfalls:
  - Forgetting that the air is compressed by depth and runs out (and fills with carbon dioxide) quickly without resupply
  - Holding your breath while rising from depth with compressed air in the lungs; the lungs can burst
  - Long work at depth followed by a fast ascent: decompression sickness (the bends, 'caisson disease' of 19th c. bridge builders)
  - Using a long snorkel tube from the surface below about 1 m; the chest cannot breathe against the water pressure
- History: greece: 4th c. BC – Aristotelian Problemata mentions a cauldron lowered to give divers air; europe: 1535 – Guglielmo de Lorena dives on the Roman ships of Lake Nemi; c. 1500 Leonardo sketches breathing apparatus; 1690s–1716 Halley's bell resupplied with air barrels; 1789 Smeaton's air-pumped bell; 1840s caissons for bridges
- Read:
  - Edmond Halley, The Art of Living Under Water, Philosophical Transactions 29, no. 349 (1716), 492–499, doi:10.1098/rstl.1714.0063
